nameStory: This lichen gets its 'curled' name from the way its edges curl and roll inward like tiny scrolls, especially when dry. The 'snow' part comes from its preference for cold, high-elevation habitats where snow lingers well into spring, and its pale coloration that helps it blend with lichen-covered rocks in these harsh environments.
description: Curled snow lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms small, cushion-like patches on rocks in New England's mountains. Its lobes are distinctly curled under at the edges, giving it a ruffled appearance like lettuce leaves that have dried out. Individual patches rarely exceed 2-3 inches across, but they can form larger colonies when growing conditions are favorable. The lichen appears pale gray-green when dry and becomes more vibrant green when wet.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Edges curl distinctly inward and downward, creating a scrolled or ruffled appearance that feels firm and leathery when touched

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, cushion-like patches of leafy lobes that overlap like shingles, creating a layered texture you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale gray-green to whitish when dry, becoming brighter green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively grows on exposed rock surfaces, particularly granite and other acidic rocks in mountainous areas

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies typically 1-3 inches across, with lobes about 1/4 inch wide that feel substantial and not papery

habitat: Look for curled snow lichen on exposed rock faces and boulders in New England's higher elevations, particularly in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and similar mountainous terrain in Vermont and Maine. It thrives on acidic rocks like granite in areas that experience long, cold winters and receive regular moisture from fog, snow, and rain. These lichens prefer spots with good air circulation but some protection from the harshest winds.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant green as snowmelt and spring rains keep it moist; curled edges may be less pronounced when well-hydrated.
seasonality.summer: Appears paler and more gray as it dries out in warmer weather; curled edges become very pronounced and crispy-feeling.
seasonality.fall: Color deepens again with increased moisture; this is often the best time to observe the contrast between wet and dry appearance.
seasonality.winter: Visible on snow-free rock faces, appearing pale and dormant but still identifiable by its distinctive curled lobes.

funFact: This tiny lichen can survive being completely frozen solid for months at a time, then wake up and resume photosynthesis within minutes of thawing - a superpower that allows it to thrive in some of New England's harshest mountain environments where most plants can't survive.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with crinkled snow lichen, but curled snow lichen has much more distinctly inward-curled edges (like scrolls) while crinkled snow lichen has wavy, wrinkled surfaces without the tight edge-rolling. Memory trick: 'curled' edges curl under like a scroll, 'crinkled' surfaces wrinkle like paper.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it only grows in snowy areas, this lichen doesn't actually require snow to survive - the 'snow' refers to its preferred cold, high-elevation habitats where snow is common, not a biological dependency on snow itself.
compareHints: Curled snow lichen differs from its close relative crinkled snow lichen primarily in the edge treatment - curled snow lichen has distinctly rolled, scroll-like edges while crinkled snow lichen has wavy, wrinkled surfaces without tight edge curling. Both prefer similar rocky, mountainous habitats, but the edge curling in this species is so pronounced it's visible even from a distance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Crinkled snow lichen differs from its close relative, curled snow lichen, by having more pronounced surface wrinkling and a more yellowish color when wet.
